text: The Keeper's Ledgers
Chapter Three: The Count
She did not catch the Thursday train. She told herself it was
because of the weather, which was true as far as it went: the
wind had gone round to the north and the ferry was not run-
ning. She spent the day carrying ledgers down to the kitchen
table, twelve at a time, and reading them in order.
Most nights were dull. A few were not. In February 1968
he had counted 43 vessels sheltering in the lee of the island
during a storm that lasted three days. In August 1979 he had
written, without comment, "Lights seen to the west at 02:10,
low on the water, not a ship." In the winter of 1985 there was
a gap of a single night, and beside it, in the margin, the
words "Influenza. Mrs. Garrity kept the count."
On Saturday the ferry ran again. Nora walked down to
the harbor, stood for some time looking at the timetable, and
then walked back up the hill. That evening, a little before
dusk, she found a pencil, opened the half-filled ledger to the
first empty page, and wrote the date at the top.
She did not know the proper way to describe the wind.
She wrote "cold, from the right." Then she pulled a chair to
the window, and waited for the first ship.
Nobody had asked her to.
